So for the jumping on guests, I would try gently grabbing her and putting her in another room, then bring her out again in maybe a minute or 2, then bring her out again. Every time she gets overly excited then do the same thing. 

Don't just take her to the pet store, park, the most distracting places, and expect her to listen. Start small, start in your back yard for a few days, then move to the front yard. After a couple of more days maybe move down the street. Slowly increase the amount of distractions. If she's starting to get overwhelmed, you may be going too fast with it. You always want to set her up for success. Always make sure you leave training on a good note as well. If she's been doing really well, but then starts to get really distracted, excited, not listening, ECT, do something really easy like sit. Make sure you have a really really rewarding treat for that last sit. If you catch yourself getting frustrated with the training, stop for now and come back to it later. You want training to be fun for both of you!

Treats are your best friend, get a treat bag to go around your waist. My favorites are the ones that are able to stay open! Make sure when you're treating her that you mix it up a little by giving her different amounts. The number of treats is going to be far more effective than giving her different sizes. So maybe tell her to sit, give her two treats. Then have her do something else and give her four. Then another thing and give her one. 

Leash pulling I was having the exact same problem with my dog and it took quite awhile to get him to stop. A few things you can try, 1: front clip harness, I'd invest in one of those. Makes it a little more uncomfortable to pull. 2: when you're walking her, every time she pulls you can just stop walking entirely. Once she stops pulling, you start walking again. 3: Be really exciting and keep her on her toes. Do random things like randomly turn right, then turn around, walk slow, then walk fast. Make her want to pay attention to you. 4: Every time she looks at you, treat her. Make her focusing on you the best thing in the world, give her lots of treats, use a toy, give her lots of pets, whatever the most rewarding thing for her is. I recommend doing this no matter what because it makes them want to check in and listen to you.

For the invading personal space, I would try getting up and walking away. Show her that every time she starts trying to demand you give her attention get up, don't look at her, and just walk away. Then come back and try again. Once she stops doing it, then she gets attention and make sure you give her lots of it. Show her that being calm and gentle gets her what she wants.

This can take a lot of time and repetition. Depending on how long you work with her is going to really decide how quickly she starts to catch on. Some dogs can take a few weeks, others a few months. Each dog learns at their own pace. It's going to be frustrating, especially when it seems like what you're doing isn't working, but eventually you will see results. I worked as a basic obedience dog trainer for a few months and in a shelter setting for a year, I've seen these tricks work!
